explanations.answer: Not to rebuke him in anger
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. David opens with “O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger or discipline me in Your wrath.” No greeting and no warm-up, he goes straight to the point. I think when you're hurting that much, small talk can wait.

explanations.answer: To give him a long life
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. A long life never comes up in this psalm. His first words are “O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger or discipline me in Your wrath.” I think he was in too much pain to ask for anything else.
That one's not in the psalm, friend. David isn't asking for fame here. He opens with “O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger or discipline me in Your wrath.” That's the first thing out of his mouth.

Yes, sin. David says, “there is no rest in my bones because of my sin.” He doesn't point at anybody else here. He owns it, and that takes some courage. He'll say it again in verse 18, so keep your ears open.
Enemies do show up in this psalm, but later, in verse 12. Here the cause he names is closer to home. He says, “there is no rest in my bones because of my sin.” He's looking at his own part.
Age never comes up in this psalm, friend. No birthdays and no candles. In verse 3, David puts it this way: “there is no rest in my bones because of my sin.” That's the reason he names.
That's right. David says, “I am bent and brought low; all day long I go about mourning.” It's not a bad hour or two. It's all day long. I think that's a heavy way to live, friend.
No cave in this psalm, friend. David never says where he is. What he does say is “all day long I go about mourning.” He goes about it, bent and brought low.
Not here, friend. This psalm has no army and no battle march. David says he's “bent and brought low,” and “all day long I go about mourning.” That's how he spends his days.

True! David says, “O Lord, my every desire is before You; my groaning is not hidden from You.” In the middle of all that pain, he knows he's heard. Nothing he groans is lost. That's worth holding onto, friend.
It's actually true, friend. The text says, “O Lord, my every desire is before You; my groaning is not hidden from You.” David isn't groaning into the empty air. He says the Lord sees every bit of it.

Yes, the light of his eyes. David says, “My heart pounds, my strength fails, and even the light of my eyes has faded.” Notice that little word “even.” The list keeps going. I think he's running on empty.

His voice isn't on the list, friend. David says, “My heart pounds, my strength fails, and even the light of my eyes has faded.” It's his eyes that go dim. He's still talking, as the whole psalm shows.

Hands aren't mentioned in that verse, friend. The verse says, “My heart pounds, my strength fails, and even the light of my eyes has faded.” The fading is in his eyes. You can double check me on that one.

It's the other way around, friend. David says, “My beloved and friends shun my disease, and my kinsmen stand at a distance.” The people closest to him keep their distance. I think that stings almost as much as the sickness.
That's right. David says, “My beloved and friends shun my disease, and my kinsmen stand at a distance.” Nobody's sitting by his bed. I think being left alone hurts on top of the pain.

explanations.answer: He does not open his mouth
explanations.explanation: Yes. David says, “like a mute man, I do not open my mouth.” He adds that he's like a man whose mouth offers no reply. While they plot, he stays quiet. Me, I can't stay quiet when a timer goes off.

explanations.answer: He shouts right back at them
explanations.explanation: Nope, it's the opposite, friend. David says, “like a mute man, I do not open my mouth.” In verse 14 he says his mouth offers no reply. No shouting at all.

explanations.answer: He makes plans to strike back
explanations.explanation: The psalm doesn't say that, friend. The plotting is on the enemies' side. David says, “like a mute man, I do not open my mouth,” and that his mouth offers no reply.

True. David says, “I wait for You, O LORD; You will answer, O Lord my God.” He's quiet toward his enemies, but he isn't quiet toward the LORD. He waits, and he says the LORD will answer. That's hope in the middle of the hurt.
It's true, friend. Verse 15 says, “I wait for You, O LORD; You will answer, O Lord my God.” His silence isn't giving up. He says plainly that he's waiting for the LORD.
Iniquity, yes. David says, “Yes, I confess my iniquity; I am troubled by my sin.” He doesn't dodge or dress it up. He just says it out loud. That's a hard thing to do, friend.
Not this time, friend. In verse 18 David isn't claiming innocence. He says, “Yes, I confess my iniquity; I am troubled by my sin.” He's owning it.
Loyalty isn't the word, friend. The verse says, “Yes, I confess my iniquity; I am troubled by my sin.” Iniquity is what he puts into words. That's what he confesses.
Not quite, friend. David says, “I am troubled by my sin.” Troubled is the opposite of at peace. He confesses it, and it still weighs on him.
That's right. David says, “Yes, I confess my iniquity; I am troubled by my sin.” He's not shrugging it off. I think it's an honest, heavy moment.

Yes. David says, “Many are my enemies without cause, and many hate me without reason.” He's not saying they have a good reason and he's ignoring it. He says they have none. Verse 20 tells us more about what they do.
The psalm doesn't say that, friend. David says, “Many are my enemies without cause, and many hate me without reason.” Battle never comes up. The text says without reason.
No land grab in this psalm, friend. David says, “Many are my enemies without cause, and many hate me without reason.” The word he uses is reason, and he says there isn't one.

explanations.answer: Not to forsake him or be far
explanations.explanation: That's it. David prays, “Do not forsake me, O LORD; be not far from me, O my God.” After all the groaning, what he wants most is the LORD close by. I think that tells us a lot, friend.

explanations.answer: To wipe out all his enemies
explanations.explanation: Not in this psalm, friend. David's request is “Do not forsake me, O LORD; be not far from me, O my God.” He asks for the LORD to stay near. Nothing about wiping anybody out.

explanations.answer: To give him back his strength
explanations.explanation: He doesn't ask for that here, friend. David prays, “Do not forsake me, O LORD; be not far from me, O my God.” His request is for the LORD's nearness. That's what he asks for.

Savior, yes. The last line is “Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior.” He ends the whole psalm with that one word for the Lord. After all the pain, that's where he lands. I'd call that a strong finish.
Not the word he uses, friend. The last line says, “Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior.” Savior is how he closes the psalm. He's asking for help.
Close to a famous psalm, but not this one, friend. The last line here says, “Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior.” Savior is the word he picks. It's a short, urgent ending.
